---
title: "Comparing The Main Methods"
---

# Purpose

This note compares the five main designs in the series on a common set of dimensions so readers can move from identification logic to design choice.

# Comparison Dimensions

## Identification Strategy

- Matching and weighting: selection on observables
- Difference-in-differences: change over time relative to comparison groups
- Synthetic control: weighted counterfactual trajectory
- Regression discontinuity: local comparison at a threshold
- Interrupted time series: a break in level or trend relative to the treated series' projected pre-intervention trajectory

## Main Assumption

- Matching and weighting: no important unobserved confounding after conditioning
- Difference-in-differences: parallel trends
- Synthetic control: strong pre-treatment fit and no treated-unit-specific confounding shocks at treatment time
- Regression discontinuity: continuity at the cutoff and no manipulation
- Interrupted time series: a credible untreated trajectory and no concurrent outcome-relevant shock at the interruption

## Data Structure

- Cross-sectional or panel for matching and weighting
- Panel or repeated cross-section for DiD
- Long panel for synthetic control
- Cross-sectional or panel with a running variable for RD
- A regularly spaced outcome series with enough observations before and after the interruption for ITS

## Diagnostic Emphasis

- Balance and overlap
- Pre-trends
- Pre-treatment fit and placebos
- Density and continuity checks
- Time plot, residual autocorrelation, seasonality, functional form, and interruption-timing checks

## Main Limitation

- Matching and weighting: hidden bias
- Difference-in-differences: trend violations
- Synthetic control: poor donor support
- Regression discontinuity: local external validity
- Interrupted time series: coincident shocks and dependence on the projected trend

# Important Boundaries

ITS, DiD, and synthetic control all use time, but they construct the counterfactual differently:

- ITS projects the treated series' own pre-intervention trajectory.
- DiD uses the change in untreated units to represent the treated units' counterfactual change.
- Synthetic control builds a weighted untreated trajectory that should reproduce the treated unit before treatment.

If a credible contemporaneous comparison series exists, a controlled ITS is usually stronger than an uncontrolled ITS. If multiple untreated units provide a plausible comparison trend, DiD may be less dependent on extrapolating one series. If one treated aggregate unit can be closely reconstructed from a donor pool, synthetic control makes the comparison more transparent.
